Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verses 1–5:

In the explanation of these words, it has been said that they refer to the angels, that is, those who pull out the souls of human beings with great force. The meaning of "nashitat" is agile and ready for work, and they float about in the furthest reaches of this universe. And they race one another in obeying the Lord and carrying out His commands, and they are engaged in managing and regulating all the affairs of this universe.

Another explanation has been given: that these refer to the stars, which sink into their orbits and the atmospheres of the universe and then emerge. They revolve at great speed, enter from one station into another. In this expanse of the universe they are suspended. Some are swift in their movement and some slow, so they outpace one another, and they carry out the commands that the hand of divine power has given them by its nature, and they affect the earth and its inhabitants; in this way they manage and regulate this earth.

According to some tafsirs, nazi'at, nashitat, sabihat and sabiqat refer to the stars, and mudabbirat are the angels; and some scholars have stated the explanation that nazi'at, nashitat and sabihat refer to the stars, while sabiqat and mudabbirat refer to the angels.

Whatever the meaning of these verses and words may be, yet living within the Qur'anic atmosphere, my sense is that the purpose of speaking in this manner and bringing these words is to awaken human feeling, to arouse curiosity within human consciousness, and to alert and awaken it to the perilous and tumultuous circumstances that are to come. These words and this meaning prepare us for what follows: that a great event is coming, which is mentioned with the words al-Tammat al-Kubra, rajifah and radifah. If we do not get entangled in the detailed meanings of these words, asking what their real intended sense is, then by thus contenting ourselves with the natural style of the Qur'an we can gain greater benefit, because the true aim of the Qur'an is to shake and warm hearts, and for this purpose the Qur'an adopts the most effective style. This is a matter from which it becomes clear how much the Companions stood in awe before the Qur'an and how greatly they respected it, as a servant respects the commands of his master and immediately obeys. Even if some words of the Qur'an are obscure and abstruse, they still have a purpose.

The answer to the matters on which the oath is sworn in the opening is the following verses; that is, the answer to the oath is depicted in these words.

On the first blast being the quaking that falls upon the earth: the reason is that in another place the trembling (rajf) is explicitly attributed to the earth.

"On the day when the quaking (tarjufu) shakes..." ﴿On the day when the earth and the mountains shall quake﴾. According to the narrations, "the following one" (al-Radifah) refers to the trembling of the sky. That is, after the earth has quaked, the sky too will tremble. It will split apart, and its stars will be scattered.

Some narrations state that "the quaker" (al-Rajifah) refers to the first Trumpet (sur). When the first Trumpet gives its harsh blast, the earth and the mountains will quake, and upon the earth beasts, animals and humans will all tremble; after this, all creatures of the heavens and the earth will fall unconscious. And "the following one" (al-Radifah) refers to the second Trumpet, through which all creatures will be brought back to life and rise from the earth, and the Plain of Gathering (maydan-e-hashr) will be established, as stated in Surah az-Zumar, verse 68.

Whatever the meaning, a tremor occurs upon the screen of human consciousness, and this depiction creates fear and anxiety in a person. Out of sheer fear, a person begins to tremble violently. Thus human consciousness comes close to grasping the terror of that day: on that day there will be such fear and agitation that even the most firm and strong person's feet will slip, and he will be restless. A person comes to understand what the meaning of this verse is.

﴿Hearts on that day will be trembling, their eyes humbled (khashi'ah)﴾ (79:9). Because these hearts will be afflicted with intense agitation, humiliation will overshadow them. The marks of fear, terror and collapse will be evident upon them. There will be an earthquake and a scene of destruction will be visible everywhere. Such collapse will likewise occur in the system of the earth and the heavens on that day.

﴿On the day when the following one follows﴾ (79:7). This scene and this picture are also conveyed by the words with which the oaths were sworn.

﴿By those who drag out violently, and those who draw out gently, and those who glide swiftly, and those who race ahead, and those who manage affairs﴾ (79:1–5). All these scenes (of the world of hearts, of this earth and sky, and of these oath-words) share one atmosphere and harmonious effects. In short, this entire surah is in the manner of a great uproar.

Now, their own impressions of that scene are quoted here, of how, after the second Trumpet is blown, they will rise suddenly and be utterly bewildered.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verses 13–14:

"Fa-innama..." to "al-sahirah" (79:14): "Indeed, it will be but a single shout, and at once they will be upon the open plain."

Al-zajr means a loud sound, that is, al-sayhah (the cry). However, here the word al-zajrah is used instead of al-sayhah, because this word is more suitable to the atmosphere and setting of this surah. The atmosphere here is one of intensity and severity. Al-sahirah refers to a white and shining earth. It means the plain of gathering (maydan al-hashr). We do not know where this plain will be. Our knowledge about it is limited to the information provided by the Truthful Informant (al-mukhbir al-sadiq, ﷺ). Therefore, we add nothing to this beyond that, because nothing other than what the Truthful Informant has said can be stated with certainty and safety.

According to the texts of the Qur'an and Sunnah, this shout refers to the second blowing of the Trumpet (al-nafkh al-sur), upon which all people will rise up from their places and from their graves. The words chosen for it show the speed of this event: that it will happen very rapidly. The events described throughout this entire surah display speed and fear. Because of this speed and fear, hearts will tremble and bodies will shudder. In this surah, every movement, every moment, and every scene and atmosphere has been arranged to maintain harmony.

Now, in the next stage, this atmosphere of speed, movement and fear gradually subsides, because in it there are only brief allusions to the story of Musa and Fir'awn. In it the end of that rebellion is shown, so the tone of the discourse becomes somewhat calmer and gentler.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verse 15:

The story of Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) is repeated many times in the Holy Qur'an, and many details of it are given. Parts of it have already passed in earlier surahs. It appears in every place with the part of the story that is needed there, in a manner and style suited to the subject and the context. In the telling of this story, the Qur'an's style of expression reaches its peak, and it is the Qur'an's distinctive method to present a story in a way that is most fitting and appropriate to its setting.

Here the story comes with great brevity, and its scenes pass swiftly like flashes. In the sacred valley of Mount Tur, Musa (peace be upon him) is called, and he is given the commands to go on a mission of preaching to Pharaoh. Mention is made of Pharaoh's rebellion, then of his evil end in this world and the Hereafter, and of God's seizing him. Thus its conclusion also harmonizes with the theme and subject of this surah, because the central theme of the surah is resurrection, gathering, and accountability. In a few short verses, with the long drawn-out rhythm of the alif, the glimpses of this story pass very quickly. Thus its manner and its impact accord with the temperament of this surah.

In these short verses, many aspects of this story are shown with great speed and swiftness.

Its beginning is made by addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿Has the story of Musa reached you?﴾ (79:15). This interrogative style is adopted so that the one addressed becomes fully attentive, all ears, to listen to the story and to grasp it completely.

After this come the details of the events. The story is referred to with the word hadith (discourse), because the story is in fact a dialogue between Musa and his Lord. Therefore, bringing the word hadith is a great display of realism: question and answer, and intimate supplication to the Lord.

"When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa" (79:16). The preferred view is that Tuwa is the name of a valley which, for one who comes from the direction of Madyan in northern Hijaz, lies on the right side of Mount Sinai (Tur).

The time at which the call came from Allah was a great and awe-inspiring moment, a time of strange states, for Allah, glorified is He, Himself was calling one of His servants. When one reflects on it, it is a momentous matter. Human words fall short of describing the terrors of those moments. It is one of the secrets of the great sovereignty and kingship of Allah. It is also one of the mysteries of the human soul: that Allah placed in the human self this capacity and made it able to hear the sublime call and to derive meaning from it. This is the last thing we can say about this station. Otherwise, understanding this station of divine discourse, its condition and its reality, is extremely difficult for a human being. It is fitting for a person to remain standing at the very edge of this station, until the time when the Lord Himself grants him the capacity to comprehend the states, manifestations, and the question and answer of this station, so that his awareness and his power of perception can taste it.

At other places the details of the dialogues between Allah and Kalim Allah (Musa, peace be upon him) at this station are also given. But in this surah, since the aim is to place brief statements around the subject, the powerful points are made here in a highly effective manner and in the form of a glimpse. Therefore, here, after only a few words, it is mentioned that the great mission was entrusted to Musa (peace be upon him). So a voice came, and the command was given.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verses 17–19:

اذھب .................... فتخشیٰ (19:79) "Go to Pharaoh, for he has indeed transgressed. And say to him: Is there in you a willingness to purify yourself, and that I guide you to your Lord so that you would fear Him?"

اذھب .................... طغی (17:79) "Go to Pharaoh, for he has indeed transgressed."

Transgression (طغیان, tughyan) is a sin that should never occur, and if it does occur, it should not be allowed to persist. It is a disliked act. It spreads corruption on the earth. Allah does not love transgression, and countless evils are born from it. Allah sent one of His most distinguished prophets, among His highest prophets, for the sole purpose of eliminating Pharaoh's transgression, and He assigned this duty by speaking Himself with that prophet. The command was given directly, and this mission was entrusted to him, so that this distinguished representative would end this evil and remove this corruption from the world. It is an extremely abhorrent act for any of the rulers to be a transgressor and a tyrant. For this reason, Allah Himself directly entrusted this mission to one of His servants, and commanded him to bring this person out of that condition and onto the paths of justice; if he did not come, then there would be justification for sending down worldly and otherworldly punishment and torment upon him.

اذھب ........................ طغی (17:79) "Go to Pharaoh, for he has become a tyrant and a transgressor." After this, Allah also teaches His servant the style in which he should present his message and call before this transgressor and tyrant's court: in an extremely gentle, attractive, and loving manner. Perhaps he will turn back, the matter will settle in his heart, and he will escape Allah's wrath and punishment.

فقل ھل .................... تزکی (18:79) "Say: Is there in you a willingness to purify yourself?" Do you desire to emerge from the filth of this transgression and tyranny, and to abandon Allah's disobediences? Do you wish to take up the path of prayer, supplication, and blessing?

واھدیک ................ فتخشی (19:79) "And I guide you to your Lord, so that you would fear Him?" Is there in you a desire to become acquainted with the ups and downs of the path to your Lord? Thus it is only said that he left Musa and continued his efforts and schemes, gathered the common people and also brought together the sorcerers. Here the Qur'an has related only one of his vile and filthy statements, which is full of ignorance, arrogance and rebellion: "I am your lord, the Most High," (we seek Allah's refuge).

This arrogant man said this statement relying on the belief that the common people are ignorant and will respond to whatever he says. The truth is that the unconditional obedience, humiliation and ignorance of the masses deceives all arrogant and dictatorial rulers gravely. Yet every arrogant ruler and dictator is in reality just a single person. He has neither power nor proof of his own. Rather, his power and proof are only this: that the humiliated and ignorant masses prostrate before him, they bow their shoulders before him, he mounts upon them, their necks keep growing longer, and he keeps pulling them with a rope. People bow their heads before him and he keeps raising himself higher. People give up their rights and their dignity in the face of him, and he keeps becoming more defiant.

Why do the common people act this way? On one side they remain deceived, and on the other side they are afraid. As for their fear, it is based merely on illusion or assumption, because every dictator and tyrant is a single individual; what can he do to thousands and hundreds of thousands of people? If people have a sense of their humanity, their dignity, their self-respect and their freedoms, then one person from among those thousands and hundreds of thousands is enough to confront that dictator. But this dictator and tyrant deceives them; he says that he is the source of authority. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verses 25–26:

After this disbelief, arrogance, denial and foul speech, the mighty powers of Allah now come into motion.

﴿So Allah seized him, [making him an example] in the Hereafter and in this world﴾ (79:25). Here the punishment of the Hereafter is placed before the punishment of this world, because the punishment of the Hereafter will be far more severe and intense. For disobedient and arrogant people, the real punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter, and in the Hereafter such people will be seized with great harshness and cruelty. Moreover, the theme of the surah is itself the Hereafter, so it was necessary to place the punishment of the Hereafter first. Also, in terms of verbal rhythm and rhyme, "al-akhirah" (the Hereafter) should have come first and "al-ula" (the first, i.e. this world) afterwards; thus both verbally and in meaning, al-akhirah and al-ula (79:25) are brought into harmony.

The punishment that Pharaoh suffered in this world was also very severe. The punishment of the Hereafter, however, will be far more intense and harsh. Pharaoh was a man of great power, and the master of family honour and dignity. If he was afflicted with such an intense punishment, then other deniers of lesser rank, dictators and rebels will certainly be afflicted with the most intense punishment. As for the polytheists of Makkah, they had no standing at all among the world powers.

﴿Indeed, in that there is a lesson for whoever fears﴾ (79:26). The one who knows Allah and fears Allah is the one who well understands what lessons lie in the story of Pharaoh for people. As for the person in whose heart there is no piety, fear or awe of Allah, veils have come between him and the lesson; a thick veil stands between him and receiving admonition. Eventually he not only meets an evil end, but goes out and collides with that evil end, and Allah takes vengeance upon him in this world and the Hereafter. Thus it is Allah who provides every person with the means of lesson, right guidance and a good end.

After this survey of dictators and those who rebel through the strength of material and political power, let us now turn to the polytheists of Makkah, who took great pride in their small power. Before them are presented some great cosmic powers, so that they may understand that, before these terrifying cosmic powers, their own strength is worthless.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verse 27:

This is a question whose answer is one and the same, one that cannot be denied and is not open to debate or argument.

﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is the sky?﴾ (79:27) "He constructed it." Surely the creation of the heavens is a great and difficult task. There is no doubt about this, and there is no room for dispute. So why are you so proud of the small strength that Allah has given you, when the sky and the other powers of the cosmos are far stronger than you? This is one aspect of the question, but it has another dimension as well: you regard your being raised again as a difficult matter, while the creation of the heavens is more difficult than your creation. Yet on the Day of Resurrection your creation will not be an original creation but merely a repetition (i'adah), and for the One Blessed Essence who created the heavens and the worlds, repeating your creation is easier.

The creation of the heavens is undoubtedly a great work.

﴿He raised it﴾ (79:27). Every building, by its strength and by its parts holding one another together, displays stability. The vast system of the heavens is likewise bound together like a building. Its stars and planets are bound within one system. Nothing moves from its place. Nothing leaves its orbit, falls, or collides. It is as though this upper universe is a vast edifice, all of whose parts are mutually held together.

"It raised its canopy high and made it proportionate" (79:28). Samk means height and stature. The sky is both elevated and tightly joined, its parts fitted together; this is what is meant by fasawwaha (79:28).

Anyone who glances at the system of the heavens, even with only a modest knowledge, realises that there is perfect harmony within the system of the heavens. What binds these great bodies together, and what organises the interplay of their movements and influences, when studied in detail, reveals the meanings of these words to be very deep and broad, and this system becomes so astonishing that people who previously knew little about it are left amazed, awestruck and bewildered. Human beings are left stunned, overawed and dumbfounded, and there is no way to explain this astonishing, vast and wide-ranging system except by acknowledging a great governing power working behind it. For humanity there is no other path to explaining this marvellous, immense and expansive system. In any case, it is necessary to acknowledge the Lord of the worlds in accordance with some religion and faith.

"And He darkens its night and brings forth its morning light." (29:79 as cited, i.e., ﴿وَأَغْطَشَ لَيْلَهَا وَأَخْرَجَ ضُحَاهَا﴾)

Note: the verse reference in the source is given as "29:79", and the quoted verse is from Surat an-Nazi'at (79:29).

Wait, I should correct that: the text is a commentary on Surah 79, verse 29, so it should be rendered as follows.

The passage, in English translation:

"And He darkens its night and brings out its forenoon brightness" (79:29). In this mode of expression, both the wording and the meaning carry intensity and rhythm, and this mode of expression fully matches the intensity and power of this surah.

﴿وَأَغْطَشَ لَيْلَهَا﴾ (79:29) means He made its night dark and black.

And ﴿وَأَخْرَجَ ضُحَاهَا﴾ (79:29) means He brought out its daylight, making the day bright. The words the Qur'an has chosen here for darkness and light are very well suited to the context of the discourse. The successive coming and going of light and darkness, the darkness of night and the brightness of forenoon, is a scene every person has seen, and every heart is affected by it. Sometimes a person, because of being too familiar with it, does not take from the turning of night and day the impression that the Qur'an describes here. But it is the excellence of the Holy Qur'an that it sharpens human sensibilities, so that a person begins to sing forgotten melodies, and all of this seems entirely new to him. It is as if each day a new day dawns. The awareness and impression that a person gains today from reading the Qur'an were not present yesterday. In light of these realities, the Qur'an awakens human sensibilities, and as human knowledge of these scenes and realities of the cosmos expands, the person's impressions, his amazement, and his awe continue to increase.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verses 30–32:

"And after that He spread out the earth, brought forth from it its water and its pasture, and set firm the mountains in it."

Dahw al-ard (spreading out the earth) means preparing the earth and spreading out its crust, so that people can walk upon it, the soil that gathers on it becomes fit to grow vegetation, and the mountains are set firmly upon it. All these matters came about in this way: Allah gave the surface of the earth stability and rest, and produced on it a degree of temperature in such a measure that animal and plant life became possible here. And Allah brought forth water from the earth, whether by this is meant the water that issues forth in the form of springs, or the water that descends from the heavens as rain and flows in the form of rivers. And through it Allah caused to grow all the vegetation from which human food and animal food come forth. Some animals eat from it directly, and some indirectly.

All this arrangement took place when Allah constructed the present system of the heavens and the earth, and created the night and the day. Modern theories about the heavens and the earth fully support the meaning of this verse: that many years passed over the earth, and the cycle of night and day continued in the same way, and afterwards it became fit for human life and agriculture, its crust hardened, and as it contracted, mountains emerged.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verse 33:

The Qur'an explicitly states that this entire system was created for your sake.

﴿As a provision for you and your cattle.﴾ (79:33) Through this, two matters are intended to be pointed out. First, that Allah has adopted magnificent arrangements for running this universe. Second, that within this system everything has been created according to a fixed formula and with a very precise measure. The giving of the present form to the heavens, the preparation of the earth in its present shape, and the existing system did not come into being by chance. Rather, it was predetermined and arranged. Each and every thing in it has been created with a reckoning and a measure, and it has been created keeping in view this very purpose: that Adam's descendants would come and settle on this earth. For its existence, its growth and its development, countless favourable conditions have been created here, and they have been placed within the basic structure and plan of this system. The whole solar system has been made in this way, and these matters have been especially kept in view within the earth.

The Qur'an's manner is to make brief indications towards the fundamental realities, which include the essential matter and truth, so that even the most ordinary person grasps the Qur'anic meaning. Here, the facilities and favourable things to which the Qur'an has pointed are: the creation and construction of the heavens; the covering of the night and its tranquil atmosphere; the appearance of the day and its bustle; the spreading out of the earth and making it habitable; the flowing of water, the growing of vegetation, the firm setting of mountains; and the providing of means of subsistence for humans and animals. Through these indications, on the one hand, the wisdom of Allah's governance and the wise order of creation become visible, and these realities are phenomena which every person sees and understands. A person of every level and every society understands them, and no great degree of knowledge is needed to understand them. Whoever is a human being, wherever he is, in whatever age he lives, understands these indications.

But if one reflects with depth behind this general level, then beneath this surface there are great realities, such as that there is deep planning in the design of the creation of this universe, and that its system does not run on mere chance and accident. The reality of this universe negates that notion, because for such a wise formula to come about merely by accident is simply not possible, which is strange and extremely wise.

The galaxy in which we live, called the Milky Way, is the galaxy of which our earth is one planet. Its organisation and its system of rotation is a wondrous system which does not exist in the tens of millions of galaxies like it. Furthermore, this earth is a planet of a unique kind among all the planets; its distance from the sun, its atmospheric conditions and its rotation are such that they make it fit for human life. To this day, humanity has not discovered in this vast and boundless universe any other planet with life of this same kind, and within which there are thousands and millions of factors that support and assist human life.

"Because the means of life are provided in a planet whose size is appropriate, which is at a suitable distance from the sun, and whose elements are composed in such a way that life can come into motion within it."

"The suitability and appropriateness of size is necessary because the atmosphere around a planet depends on how large the planet is and how strong its gravitational force is."

"And a moderate distance is necessary because planets that are closer to the sun are so hot that the constituent parts of bodies cannot remain in their place, and planets that are very far from the sun are so cold and solid that no body can flourish or thrive within them."

"Furthermore, it is necessary that a planet be composed of elements in which life is possible and can flourish, because the elements that are present on this earth are necessary for plants and animals."

"Then the earth has been placed at such a distance from the sun that if its distance were to vary even slightly, life on it would not be possible at all. We now know its details well. To this day we have not been able to determine that any other planet revolves around any sun in such a way."

(Thinkers of the Twentieth Century, Ustadh Aqqad, p. 32.)

These realities, that this universe has been made according to a specific order, plan and design, and that within it humanity holds a particular station, incline a person towards the conclusion that the Establishment of the Hour is a reality, and that a day is coming when humans will be held to account and will be requited for their deeds with reward and punishment. If the creation of this universe and of human life within it conforms to a wise manner, then necessarily a person will reach the conclusion that this life will one day come to an end, and that humans will face the requital of their deeds. It would be extremely unreasonable and unjust if the end of this life were such that the oppressors and wrongdoers escape punishment, and the oppressed, after bearing hardships in the world, are simply brought to an end. Beliefs and ideas of this kind are contrary to the wisdom, the planning and the design that are evident in the creation and making of this universe.

For this very reason, after these realities, the central theme of the surah, namely the Establishment of the Hour, is now taken up: that great upheaval which will take place, and after which this world will come to an end. Before this, minds had been prepared to accept this belief. The mind was ready for acceptance. Therefore this mention came at a most appropriate time.

This worldly life is but a few days, and for it a system of life and means of living have been prepared here with profound depth and wisdom. Between the order of this universe and the order of human life there is a deep connection. Yet despite this, it is a fleeting possession, and one day it must come to an end. When that great upheaval takes place, the system of this life will be suspended. This brief life will end. This vast universe will end. These lofty heavens, these towering mountains, this wide and expansive earth, and all the struggles and activities that take place upon it, will all come to an end, because that event will be very great and very all-encompassing. It will engulf everything.

Now man will remember what he has been doing; now all his activities will come back to him one after another. The events of his life will come back to him. The preoccupations of life that had made man heedless of that great day will now be entirely known to him. But now this recollection will give him nothing except regret and despair. **Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verse 36:**

"And Hellfire will be made visible to everyone who sees" (79:36). Now it will not be hidden from sight. Every beholder will be able to see it. In the word "burrizat" (برزت), both the verbal emphasis (tashdid) and the meaning-based emphasis are intended. Through this word a scene is brought before every eye, and then there is also the resonance of the word itself.

Today everyone's end will differ, and the system of the universe, the system of trial, and the purposes of the first life will become fully clear.

Then as for one who transgressed and preferred the life of this world, indeed Hellfire will be his refuge (79:37–39).

The meaning of tughyan (transgression) and sarkashi (rebellion) is broader. It applies to every person who oversteps the path of truth and guidance. Its scope is wider than that of those rebellious oppressors who transgress through force, coercion and absolute authority. Everyone who is worldly-minded and strays from the path of guidance in various directions is a transgressor (tagut). The defining trait of the rebel and transgressor is that he gives preference to this world over the Hereafter, and pays no heed to accountability before the Hereafter. The truth is that concern for the Hereafter is what creates balance between a person's conscience and his conduct. If someone forgets the Hereafter, or puts the world ahead of it, then a rift arises between his values and his standards, and all his criteria and values change. His consciousness and his way of life change. Consequently, he becomes a rebel and a transgressor, exceeding limits and committing oppression. Thus his end is this: "Hellfire becomes his refuge." That Hellfire which lay open and present, and which was made manifest on the Great Day.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verse 40:

﴿And as for one who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from [its] desire, then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.﴾ (79:40-41)

One who fears standing before his Lord does not commit any sin. If, through human weakness, a lapse occurs from him, this fear compels him to remorse and seeking forgiveness; he repents, and thus he re-enters the sphere of obedience.

To restrain the soul from desires means that a person does not step outside the sphere of obedience, because it is the desires of the self that incite human beings to disobedience, transgression and rebellion. The paths of trial and of Satan are none other than the desires of the self. Satan attacks a person through this very path. The cure for ignorance is very easy, but to follow the desires of the self knowingly is a very great affliction and trial, and to confront it requires great struggle.

The pressure of the desires of the self can be confronted only with the fear of God. No weapon other than the fear of Allah can confront this enemy. This is why the Qur'an has combined them in a single verse. And who is speaking? The Being who created the human self. He both tells the disease and the cure. Its Creator alone is aware of the ups and downs of the human self. That Being knows in which places in this creation there are weaknesses and what their cure is, and how these hidden weaknesses can be pursued, and what the methods for doing so are.

Allah the Exalted has not made man responsible for having no desire within his self; rather, Allah has commanded that he restrain the self, bridle it, and keep its desires somewhat in check. And in this matter he should seek assistance through the fear of God, [remembering] that one day he has to stand before the Lord of Majesty. And if he controls the desires of his self, its reward for him will be Paradise, and this will be his abode.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 79, verse 41:

﴿Then as for one who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the self from [its] desire, then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge﴾ (79:40-41). Because Allah knows that the struggle against the self (jihad al-nafs) is the greatest jihad, and its price is that the self becomes upright and reaches a lofty station and rank.

Man is truly man only when he acts upon this prohibition: he struggles against the self and thereby raises himself from a fallen level. A person does not become human by surrendering his self to its desires, pursuing them wherever he can, and then offering as justification that Allah placed these desires in his nature. For the One who placed the turmoil of carnal desires within the human self is the same One who gave man the power to bridle the runaway self. He also commanded that one not follow every desire of the self, that one extricate oneself from its sphere of attraction and pull, and He announced the reward: your lasting abode will be in Paradise, if you struggle against the self and prevail, and rise to loftiness, you will enter Paradise.

There is one kind of human freedom through which Allah has honoured man: it is the freedom to conquer one's own self and to be liberated from enslavement to the desires of the self, and to maintain a balanced attitude towards the self that is in harmony with human freedom, free will and destiny. But what is nowadays called human freedom is in reality animal freedom. In it, a person bows his knees before the desires of his self and becomes a slave; the reins are not in his hand but in the hands of his self's desires. It is only those who are defeated, who are slaves, who speak of such freedoms; yes, they have inscribed the title of "freedom" upon the garb of slavery, and named madness "wisdom."

Only the person endowed with the first freedom is truly elevated, progressive, and free, and entitled to a noble life, whose station is in Jannat al-Ma'wa. The person endowed with the second freedom is in reality fallen, a slave to the desires of the self, with his knees bowed before them. His true station is the depths of Hell, where humanity ends, and such a person will become fuel for Hell like trees and stones. This is a stone, not a human being.

In this religion, this is the criterion of decline and backwardness, and of elevation and progress, where things and deeds are given their true weight.

Now in this surah a sharp blow is struck upon the strings of reason and understanding, from which a long melody rises.

[Passage from "یسئلونک" to "اوضحھا" — Qur'anic verses]

The polytheists, drowned in obstinacy, when they heard from the tongue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) these terrors of the Day of Resurrection, and heard in the Qur'an the great events of the Hour's establishment, and the turmoil and great uproar, that there would be reckoning, recompense and punishment, would immediately ask a question.

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will be its appointed time?﴾ (79:42) "When will that Hour finally arrive and settle?" This was their question.

"The answer is this.

"Why are you [concerned] with mentioning it?" (79:43). This is a reply which shows that it is something very great and a momentous event, and that asking about it in this manner by these people is foolishness and baseness. It is a childish question, and a matter beyond their limits and station. So instead of answering them, the answer is given to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "What is your concern that you should state its time?" This is far greater than that you should ask about it, or be asked about it. Stating its time, or causing it to come about, is the affair of my Lord, not my affair."

The Qur'anic phrase is ﴿إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ مُنتَهَاهَا﴾ (79:44), and the passage reads:

"Its knowledge rests with Allah." Its matter comes to a halt with Allah; it is He alone who knows the time of its establishment. And it is He who determines its appointed time.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 79, verse 45:

"You are only a warner to those who fear it" (79:45). Your duty is only this. Your limits extend only so far: to warn the one who fears the Hour. That is, those people who believe that one day they will have to appear before God. That day will certainly come, and knowledge of its time belongs to Allah alone.

Yes, instead of telling the time, its horrors and tumults are described. And when it comes to pass, what will the human consciousness be at that moment, and how will the feelings be? Gauge its greatness from this alone: at that time you will express these impressions about this entire worldly life.

"On the day they see it, it will seem to them as though they had tarried but an evening or a morning of a single day." (79:46)

On the Qur'anic verse, there are impressions to be had like this: upon seeing its greatness, you will regard the entire world, your entire lifetimes, and all your belongings as though they were but a brief span of a morning and evening that we spent in the world.

This world, for which people fight and quarrel with one another, and over which they have waged an all-encompassing struggle against each other. The people of this world die, and for its sake they abandon the everlasting and boundless rewards of the Hereafter, and for this brief period they commit grave crimes and oppression, they disobey, they rebel, and night and day they are immersed in its pursuit. This world will shrink and contract in the eyes of these worldly people to such an extent that they will say: we remained only for as long as a short portion of the morning or a portion of the evening.

This is the world: brief, quickly passing away, insignificant and impermanent, low in value and inferior. Do people abandon eternal life and its blessings for the sake of a brief span of this world, about which their own impression will be that it was not even equal to a full day, but rather equal to only a portion of morning or evening? Even the desires of this world are desires that will vanish.

The truth is that man is afflicted with a great foolishness. No person of sound intellect and seeing eyes could commit such an act.
